# A fresh deployment is open, and the first key closes it

A rimsky deployment with no api keys in its ledger is in anonymous mode: it
answers every operator action with no credential presented. Minting the first
admin key closes that window immediately, and the minted key restores everything
the anonymous caller could do.

## Before the first key

Bring up a deployment and ask it what mode it is in.

```bash
export BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8080
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/auth/status"
# {"mode":"anonymous"}
```

A complete operator lifecycle runs unauthenticated — register a template, deploy
it, create an instance, read it, terminate it:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/v1/templates" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"spec":{"name":"demo","version":"1","nodes":[{"type":"worker","executor":"http-node"}]}}'
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/v1/templates/$TPL/deploy" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}'
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/v1/instances" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"template":"'"$TPL"'","instance_key":"demo-1","target_agent":"my-agent"}'
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID"
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID/terminate" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

Across the whole published control-API route set, the anonymous caller meets no
authorization refusal: routes answer 2xx, 400 for an empty body, or 404 for an
identifier that does not exist.

One route is a deliberate exception. On a deployment configured for mTLS peer
auth, `POST /v1/enroll` refuses the anonymous caller with 403 and a message
naming the missing authenticated principal, while `GET /v1/ca-root` answers 200
to the same caller.

## Mint the first key

```bash
rimsky auth init --endpoint "$BASE"
```

The verb mints the first admin key and prints its plaintext once. Capture it —
no verb retrieves it afterwards.

## After the first key

Re-run any of the calls above with no credential:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "$BASE/v1/instances"
# 401
```

Every control-API route now answers 401 to an unauthenticated caller except
`GET /v1/health`, which stays open so a container orchestrator can still probe
liveness. The close needs no restart, no configuration edit and no second act:
the mint is the switch.

Present the key and the surface comes back whole:

```bash
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" "$BASE/v1/auth/status"
# {"mode":"authenticated", ...}
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" "$BASE/v1/instances"
curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  "$BASE/v1/templates" -d '{"spec":{...}}'
```

On the mTLS deployment, the same `POST /v1/enroll` that refused the anonymous
caller answers 200 for the key. Locking down costs the operator the credential
and nothing else.

## What anonymous mode does not have

No configuration key turns anonymous mode off. `anonymous_mode: false`,
`auth: {required: true}`, `require_auth: true`, `anonymous: {enabled: false}`
and `auth_mode: required` each stop the container at startup with
`field <name> not found`; the environment variables of the same shape are
ignored and the deployment comes up open. The mode is derived from the data —
the ledger has zero active keys — so the window stays open until a key exists.

What the deployment gives instead is a WARN banner at startup naming the state,
the immediate flip the moment `rimsky auth init` runs, and a guard on the way
back: revoking the last remaining key answers 409 unless the request carries
`?force_leave_anonymous=true`.
